narr: Welcome to this section on ethical and design rules in engineering. We'll explore the professional standards that guide engineers and the systematic approaches to design problems.
Let's start with the ethical rules that every engineer should follow.

data.heading: The Six NSPE Canons
bullets: The safety/health/welfare of the public is paramount
Practice only within your area of competence
Public statements are objective and truthful
Be a faithful agent or trustee
Act honorably and lawfully — for the honor of the profession

narr: The National Society of Professional Engineers provides six fundamental canons that form the bedrock of engineering ethics. The most important of these is that the safety, health, and welfare of the public must always be paramount.
Engineers must also practice only within their area of competence, ensuring they have the necessary knowledge and experience for their work.
When making public statements, engineers must remain objective and truthful, avoiding any misleading information.
As professionals, engineers must act as faithful agents or trustees for their clients and employers.
Deception in any form is strictly prohibited in engineering practice.
Finally, engineers must always act honorably and lawfully, upholding the dignity and reputation of the profession.

data.heading: The Extended Ten Ethical Rules
bullets: No hidden payments from several parties
Do not stay silent about violations of standards even under pressure

narr: Building on the six NSPE canons, there are four additional ethical rules that extend the professional standards. These include avoiding any hidden payments from multiple parties that could create conflicts of interest.
Engineers must never misrepresent their own qualifications, experience, or the results of their work.
When collaborating, proper credit must be given to all co-authors for their contributions.
Perhaps most importantly, engineers should not remain silent when they observe violations of professional standards, even when facing pressure to do so.

data.heading: Five Cornerstones of Personal Ethics
bullets: Do not disclose what was entrusted to you
Do not take part in lies

narr: Beyond professional codes, personal ethics forms the foundation of engineering integrity. The first cornerstone is fulfilling your commitments and doing what you promised to do.
Confidentiality is essential—engineers must not disclose information that has been entrusted to them.
When things go wrong, engineers must accept responsibility rather than shifting blame.
Honesty is non-negotiable—engineers should never participate in lies or deceptive practices.
Finally, engineers should avoid accepting gifts that could compromise their professional judgment or create conflicts of interest.
As a supplement to these cornerstones, the golden rule—treating others as you would want to be treated—provides additional ethical guidance.

data.heading: Ethical Decision-Making Tools
bullets: The top question: 'Would I do this in front of my mother?'
The ethical decision matrix: evaluating actions against canons

narr: When faced with ethical dilemmas, engineers can use simple yet powerful decision-making tools. A straightforward question to ask yourself is: 'Would I do this in front of my mother?' This personal test often reveals ethical issues.
For more complex decisions, the ethical decision matrix provides a systematic approach. In this matrix, rows represent the ethical canons, and columns represent different courses of action.
For each canon-action combination, you evaluate whether the action is acceptable with a yes, no, or maybe response, providing justification for each decision.
After filling the matrix, you sum the yes and no responses (ignoring maybes), keeping in mind that one overriding criterion can cancel out the count.
This structured approach helps ensure that ethical considerations are thoroughly examined before making important decisions.

data.heading: Course-Specific Ethical Rules
bullets: Attendance: ≥75% to be admitted to the final
Plagiarism: 1st offense — 0 and possible resit, 2nd — 0 without resit, 3rd — course failure
AI assistance: allowed with explicit citation and description of contribution
AI-generated text: submitting as your own is an academic violation

narr: In this course, specific ethical rules apply to academic conduct. First, attendance is mandatory—you need at least 75% attendance to be admitted to the final examination.

Plagiarism is taken very seriously. A first offense results in a zero grade with possible resubmission, a second offense means a zero without resubmission, and a third offense leads to course failure.
While AI assistance is permitted, it must be properly cited with explicit mention of the tool used and a clear description of its contribution to your work.
Submitting AI-generated text as your own work without proper attribution is considered an academic violation and will be treated as plagiarism.

data.heading: Design Problem Characteristics
bullets: Open-ended and ill-structured: no single answer
'Best' is determined by the client's critical requirements

narr: Engineering design problems differ from typical academic problems in important ways. First, they are open-ended and ill-structured, meaning there is no single correct answer.
Instead, the 'best' solution is determined by the client's critical requirements and constraints, which must be carefully identified and prioritized.
This means that engineering design requires not just technical knowledge but also understanding of stakeholder needs and effective decision-making processes.

data.heading: Problem Definition Principles
bullets: Define the problem in terms of needs, not solutions
A solution in the statement closes the door on other solutions

narr: A crucial principle in design problem definition is to focus on needs rather than solutions. This means clearly identifying what the client actually needs to accomplish.
If you include a specific solution in the problem statement, you inadvertently close the door on potentially better alternative approaches.
By keeping the problem statement solution-neutral, you maintain maximum flexibility for creative problem-solving and innovation.

data.heading: The Eight Steps of the Design Process (Kosky)

narr: The Kosky design process provides a systematic approach to engineering problems with eight distinct steps. The first step is to clearly define the problem, ensuring you understand the actual needs.
Once the problem is defined, the next step is to generate multiple alternative solutions, avoiding premature attachment to any single approach.
After generating alternatives, you evaluate and select the most promising option based on established criteria.
The detail step involves fleshing out the chosen solution with specific specifications and implementation plans.
Before moving forward, you must defend your design decision, justifying why it meets the requirements and constraints.
With a defended design, you proceed to build and test a prototype or model to verify its functionality.
After testing, you evaluate performance against the original requirements and identify areas for improvement.
Finally, the process concludes with a comprehensive final report documenting the entire design journey and results.

data.heading: Goals of a Systematic Design Approach
bullets: Maximum thinking and information gathering before the final choice

narr: A systematic approach to design serves two important goals. First, it helps remove personal biases that might otherwise influence decision-making.
Second, it encourages maximum thinking and information gathering before making the final choice, leading to more robust and effective solutions.
By following a structured process, engineers can ensure that all relevant factors are considered and that decisions are based on evidence rather than intuition alone.

data.heading: Design Notebook Requirements
bullets: Do not rewrite a fair copy

narr: A design notebook is an essential tool for documenting the engineering design process. Pages should be numbered and dated to establish a chronological record.
Never tear pages out of a design notebook, as this can create suspicion about what might have been removed.
Unlike formal reports, design notebooks should not be rewritten as fair copies—they should capture the actual thinking process, including mistakes and dead ends.
Always use pen rather than pencil, as it's more permanent and cannot be erased.
When making corrections, strike through errors rather than erasing them, preserving a record of the thought process.
Printouts and other materials should be pasted into the notebook rather than clipped or stapled.
Write as if another reader will need to understand your work, ensuring clarity and completeness.
Finally, record all meetings and discussions related to the design project, noting who was present and what was decided.

data.heading: Brainstorming Rules
bullets: No criticism while ideas are being offered
One person speaks at a time
Do not tie an idea to a person
Afterwards: shortlist promising ideas without detailed evaluation

narr: Brainstorming is a technique for generating creative solutions to design problems. The first rule is to prohibit criticism while ideas are being offered, creating a safe space for creativity.
Only one person should speak at a time to ensure that all ideas are heard clearly.
A designated facilitator helps guide the process, keeping the discussion focused and productive.
Everything said during brainstorming should be written down, capturing even the seemingly impractical ideas.
Crucially, ideas should not be attributed to specific individuals, encouraging free thinking without fear of personal judgment.
After the initial brainstorming session, the team should shortlist the most promising ideas, but without detailed evaluation at this stage—evaluation comes later in the process.

data.heading: Team Versus Group
bullets: A team shares a common goal and coordinates effectively
The leader delegates, communicates, maintains humor and confidence, and sets an example

narr: In engineering contexts, there's an important distinction between a team and a simple group. A team is characterized by a shared goal and effective coordination among members.

Effective team leadership involves several key functions: delegating appropriate tasks, maintaining clear communication, keeping team morale high with humor and confidence, and setting an example through professional conduct.
These elements combine to create a productive team environment where engineering work can flourish.

data.heading: Project Management 3S (Dym)
bullets: Scope: defining what is and isn't included in the project
Tools: Gantt charts and PERT networks

narr: Effective project management in engineering follows the 3S framework developed by Clive Dym. The first S stands for scope—clearly defining what is and isn't included in the project.
The second S is schedule—establishing realistic timelines and deadlines for project milestones.
The third S represents spending—carefully managing the project budget to ensure resources are used efficiently.

To implement these 3S elements, engineers use specialized tools like Gantt charts, which display task bars over time to visualize project schedules, and PERT networks, which map out task dependencies and identify the critical path.

data.heading: Client Statement Analysis
bullets: Look for errors, biases, and implied solutions
Cross out the means for the time being

narr: When analyzing a client's initial statement, engineers must look for potential errors, biases, and any implied solutions that might limit creative thinking.

A systematic approach is to sort all attributes into four categories: Objectives (what the client wants to achieve), Constraints (limitations that must be respected), Features (specific elements the client desires), and Metrics (how success will be measured).
Importantly, any specified means or approaches should be crossed out temporarily, as they might prematurely constrain the solution space.
This careful analysis ensures that the design process focuses on actual needs rather than assumed solutions.

data.heading: Functions via the Black Box
bullets: 'Lift the lid' to understand internal processes
Listing tricks: 'what if X disappeared?' and 'how do you maintain it over the life cycle?'

narr: The black box approach is useful for understanding system functions. First, identify and list all the inputs and outputs of the system without considering the internal workings.
Then, 'lift the lid' to explore the internal processes and mechanisms that transform inputs into outputs.

Two helpful techniques can deepen this analysis: asking 'what if X disappeared?' to test the importance of each component, and considering 'how do you maintain it over the life cycle?' to ensure long-term viability.
This systematic approach ensures comprehensive understanding of system functions before detailed design begins.
Now let's examine the course project milestones that guide your engineering design work throughout the semester.
These milestones represent key deliverables that demonstrate your progress through the design process.
Milestone 1, due in weeks 2-3, requires you to finalize your chosen system and clearly define its boundaries.
Your system must have at least three inputs and three outputs to demonstrate a complete understanding of its function.
You'll create a stakeholder map identifying who Uses, Runs, or is Affected by the system.
This milestone also requires a Process Flow Diagram (PFD) that illustrates how the system operates.
Together, these components constitute your submissible Milestone 1 deliverable.
Milestone 2, in week 5, shifts focus to problem formulation. You'll develop a comprehensive problem statement document that clearly articulates what needs to be solved.
Alongside this, you'll provide an explicit list of all modeling assumptions that will guide your approach to solving the problem.
These documents ensure that everyone has a shared understanding of the problem and the constraints under which you'll be working.

data.heading: Milestone 3 (Week 7)
bullets: First quantitative pass of the model

narr: By week 7, Milestone 3 requires you to complete your first quantitative pass of the model, moving from qualitative to quantitative analysis.
You'll also prepare and deliver a short pitch presentation in class, summarizing your approach and preliminary results.
This milestone demonstrates your ability to translate conceptual designs into mathematical models and communicate your work effectively.

data.heading: Milestone 4 (Week 10)
bullets: Trade-off analysis of at least two alternative designs

narr: Milestone 4 in week 10 involves conducting a thorough trade-off analysis comparing at least two alternative design approaches.
This analysis should evaluate the alternatives against multiple criteria, helping to justify your final design decisions.
The trade-off analysis demonstrates your ability to make informed engineering decisions based on systematic evaluation.
Milestone 5 in week 12 requires you to develop a draft scenario simulation that models how your design would perform in different conditions.
You'll then compare the outcomes of these scenarios to validate your design and identify potential improvements.
This milestone represents the final validation step before completing your comprehensive design project.

data.heading: Lab Grading Criteria
bullets: Lab 2: Graded on all six systems steps
Lab 4: Graded on all three parts of the template (A: classification and framing; B: process and variables; C: stakeholders and goals)

narr: The labs in this course are graded using specific criteria. Lab 2 is graded based on completion of all six systems steps as outlined in the assignment.
Lab 4 is evaluated on all three parts of the provided template: Part A (classification and framing), Part B (process and variables), and Part C (stakeholders and goals).
These live checklist evaluations ensure that you're developing the systematic thinking skills essential for engineering practice.
Now let's review the course assignments for the first four weeks of the semester.
The independent work is structured around a continuous team project, with both group and individual tasks supporting your learning objectives.

rows.text: Individual reflection: identify three everyday systems, describe their boundaries and stakeholders — preparation for choosing the team system (announced at the end of lecture 1: a laundromat, a bus route, a cafeteria, a payment app)
Team task: finalize the choice of system; sketch the boundary and the stakeholder map (draft Milestone 1; announced at lecture 2: at least 3 inputs and 3 outputs)
Lab 2 "Applied Systems Challenge": six steps on the conflict card (system name, boundary, inputs/outputs, stakeholders, decision, context)
Team deliverable: a full process flow diagram and stakeholder map — submit (Milestone 1)

narr: Here's an overview of the assignments for weeks 1-3. Each week includes 4 hours of independent work as specified in the syllabus.

In week 1, you have an individual reflection assignment where you identify three everyday systems and describe their boundaries and stakeholders. This prepares you for choosing the team system, with examples like a laundromat, bus route, cafeteria, or payment app provided.
The deadline for this reflection is before lecture 2 in week 2.

In week 2, there's a team task to finalize your system choice and sketch the boundary and stakeholder map, which constitutes a draft of Milestone 1. This requires at least 3 inputs and 3 outputs as specified in lecture 2.

Also in week 2, Lab 2 is an "Applied Systems Challenge" where your team will complete six steps on a conflict card covering system name, boundary, inputs/outputs, stakeholders, decision, and context. This lab is graded in class during the lab session.
Finally, in week 3, your team will submit a full process flow diagram and stakeholder map as Milestone 1.
These assignments build systematically upon each other, guiding you through the initial phases of the engineering design process.
